video_title: How To Save a Child's Life From Gaza
transcript: This isn't going to be a normal video from me. This is going to be a much more personal video in which I've partnered with the Palestine Children's Relief Fund or PCRF to explain to you how they've managed to evacuate children from Gaza since the war there began and why they need my help and your help to continue their mission saving more children. PCRF has maintained a treatment abroad program for decades, long before the current war began and have sent thousands of Palestinian children from the West Bank and Gaza abroad for medical treatment. But after the current unprecedented war exploded in and around Gaza after October 7th, 2023, the scale of human suffering in the region reached even more unprecedented heights. And regardless of how you feel about this conflict, I believe that the children caught up in the middle of it are universally innocent victims of the events surrounding them that they have had no say, influence, or part of in causing. When the war began, roughly half of Gaza's entire population were estimated to have been children younger than the age of 18, numbering some 1 million in their entirety. And 330,000 of those were believed to be very young children below the age of five. And over the past three years of total war in Gaza, every single one of these children have experienced unbelievable horrors that will haunt and torment them for the rest of their lives. Over the span of about 2 years during the war between January of 2024 and February of 2026, PCRF managed to successfully evacuate more than 300 children from Gaza and the West Bank who were in urgent need of medical treatment to other countries around the world. And all of this while just using a small team on a shoestring budget that was only costing 1.6% of PCRF's entire budget. The team was run by Turk Hat. currently director of strategic engagement at PCRF and the former director of their treatment abroad program from their office in the United States, while the team down on the ground assisted with ambulance logistics and paperwork within Gaza. All in all, the team tracked child patients they wanted to evacuate using a master intake database. By the end, this database held 1,287 children's names, with nearly half of them being new cases logged throughout the course of the war. As the war and its circumstances have evolved over the years, the strategies and methods employed by PCRF and evacuating the children from this list had to evolve alongside of them. Ultimately, three primary logistical methods of getting children out of Gaza were developed by PCRF with each new one opening up because the last one had been shut down. And I want to tell you the story of each of these three methods using the personal real life stories of one child per method. The first method tells the story of Fi Alzant. Born in Gaza on the 19th of December of 2017, Fi was only 6 years old when the war erupted in late 2023. He was also born with cystic fibrosis, a rare inherited genetic disorder that causes mucus throughout the body to become unusually thick and sticky, which causes a multitude of serious lifelong side effects. Most notably, cystic fibrosis prevents digestive enzymes from being able to effectively reach the intestines. which causes food to only be partially broken down and nutrients to be poorly absorbed. People and especially children who have cystic fibrosis are therefore dramatically more prone to malnutrition. Before the war, Fonnie lived with his mother Shya and his twin brother Hamdan in the Al-Naser neighborhood of northern Gaza. His favorite thing to do was spending time with his grandparents who lived in the same building. He would spend hours a day sitting and chatting with his grandfather. And despite his medical condition, which kept him out of school and away from a normal childhood, Fi was always full of life and was always talking. And then in October of 2023, the war began and everything changed for the worse. As the destruction in Gaza escalated and the siege intensified, Fi lost access to a cystic fibrosis medication known as Creon, which helps him digest his food along with his nutritional supplements. Under ideal circumstances, because of their difficulty in digesting food, cystic fibrosis patients require three times the normal human's caloric intake. But as the scourge of famine began setting into Gaza along with the loss of his medication, Fi's cystic fibrosis was effectively a death [music] sentence. He began literally simply wasting away. He lost so much weight that at his lowest, he weighed only 25 lb, less than the weight of a 2-year-old toddler at his age of six. Chima, his mother, despared at the worsening plight of her children. One day, she attempted to give F a bath, but when she lifted him, his body was so fragile she was terrified he would literally shatter in her arms. His energy and life seemed almost completely gone. And it was then emotionally broken that F's family decided that they would risk everything to try and get him to a hospital. This was an incredibly difficult and dangerous decision for them to take in the middle of an all-out war. They had no car and no transportation of any kind available to them other than their own feet. Most of the hospitals in Gaza were by this point inoperable because of the damage they had sustained during the war. [music] And they had to walk for more than 3 hours to the nearest one that still had some functionality left. The doctors there rushed him to their remaining machines, but his condition remained critical and continued worsening. His story began being widely shared and it was eventually brought to the attention of PCRF. He was identified, logged into their intake database, and they immediately began getting to work on getting him out to safety. Tar and his team at PCRF reached out to Shya and helped guide the family along the process of filling out the Ministry of Health referral form. The critical document required to kickstart the official process. This step was important because it had to come from the Ministry [music] of Health and not from a private hospital or an NGO clinic. The distinction between the two was learned by PCRF the hard way in March of 2024 when another child in their system, [music] Ibrahim Abuda, was physically turned away from the border at Rafa because his documentation came from a private hospital rather than from the Ministry of Health. Alongside this mandatory form the PCRF helped compile for FOD, they also helped to provide his full medical records and cystic fibrosis diagnosis, condition photographs, referral reports in both English and Arabic, signed consent from his mother, Shima, [music] to evacuate him and receive medical treatment abroad, passport information along with child and companion identification documents.
